title: Olbers' Paradox: Why Is the Night Sky Dark?
question: If the universe is vast and full of stars, why isn't every point in the night sky blazing with light?
summary: How the simple darkness between the stars turns out to be evidence that the universe has a finite age, is expanding, and is far from equilibrium.
content:
In 1823, Heinrich Olbers sharpened a puzzle that had nagged astronomers since Kepler: if the universe is infinite, eternal, and evenly filled with stars, then every line of sight from Earth should eventually end on the surface of a star. The night sky should not be dark. It should blaze, everywhere, with the brightness of the Sun's surface. That it doesn't is one of the simplest observations in science, and one of the deepest.

Why the Paradox Bites

The argument is geometric. Imagine the sky divided into thin concentric shells around us. A shell twice as far away is dimmer per star by a factor of four (the inverse-square law), but it holds four times as many stars, because its surface area grows with the square of the distance. Each shell contributes the same total light. Add infinitely many shells and you get infinite brightness, or, once nearer stars block farther ones, a sky uniformly as bright as a stellar surface.

The obvious escape, that dust absorbs the distant light, fails. In an eternal universe the dust would absorb energy until it heated up and glowed as brightly as the stars themselves. Something about the assumptions has to give.

The Real Answer: The Universe Has a History

The resolution is that the universe is neither infinitely old nor static. Because the observable universe began roughly 13.8 billion years ago, light from sufficiently distant regions simply hasn't had time to reach us. Our line of sight runs out of stars before it runs into one. Strikingly, the first person to propose something like this answer was not a physicist but Edgar Allan Poe, who wrote in his 1848 prose poem Eureka that the dark gaps in the sky could be explained only if light from the distant regions had not yet arrived.

Expansion adds a second effect. Light from distant galaxies is stretched to longer wavelengths as space expands, losing energy along the way. The most distant light we see at all, the cosmic microwave background, was emitted when the whole universe was a glowing plasma about as hot as the surface of a red star. In a sense Olbers was right: in every direction, our line of sight does end on a glowing surface. That surface has just been redshifted by a factor of about 1,100, from orange-hot visible light into microwaves at 2.7 kelvin.

Darkness as Evidence

This is what makes the paradox beautiful. The darkness between the stars is not an absence of information; it is data. Any child looking up can see, in principle, that the universe had a beginning, or at least that it is not infinite, eternal, and unchanging all at once. Cosmologists like to point out that the dark night sky was arguably the first observational evidence for something like the Big Bang, available centuries before Hubble.

It also connects to thermodynamics. A universe at equilibrium would be uniformly bright; the dark sky is a sign that the universe is far from equilibrium, with hot stars set against a cold background. That temperature difference is what powers every process on Earth, from photosynthesis to thought. The darkness of night and the possibility of life are the same fact seen from two angles.

A Lesson in Hidden Assumptions

Olbers' paradox is a model for how good puzzles work. Each assumption (infinite space, infinite time, uniformity, a static cosmos) seems harmless on its own. The contradiction forces you to discover which one is false, and the answer turns out to be one of the largest facts about reality.

perspectives.title: Cosmology Perspective
perspectives.description: The finite age of the universe limits how far we can see, and cosmic expansion redshifts distant light. The cosmic microwave background is the glowing 'surface' Olbers predicted, cooled to 2.7 K.

perspectives.title: Thermodynamics Perspective
perspectives.description: A dark sky means the universe is out of equilibrium: hot stars against a cold background. That gradient is the energy source for every complex structure, including life.

perspectives.title: History of Science Perspective
perspectives.description: Kepler, Halley, and Olbers wrestled with the puzzle; Edgar Allan Poe guessed the right answer in 1848, and Lord Kelvin later made it quantitative. A simple question outlived several worldviews.

perspectives.title: Philosophy of Science Perspective
perspectives.description: The paradox shows how a contradiction exposes hidden assumptions. Infinite, eternal, uniform, static: each is plausible alone, but together they are refuted by looking up.
